what_its_for: Betamethasone is a corticosteroid (steroid) medicine used to reduce swelling, redness, itching, and irritation. It can be used to treat skin conditions like eczema, psoriasis, rashes, and allergic reactions. It also comes as an injection used to help speed up a baby's lung development when there is a risk of early delivery, or to treat joint pain and inflammation.
how_to_take:
How you take betamethasone depends on the form your doctor prescribed: 
• CREAM, OINTMENT, OR LOTION: Wash and dry the affected skin area. Apply a thin layer of the cream, ointment, or lotion to the affected area and gently rub it in. Wash your hands before and after applying, unless you are treating your hands. Do not cover the treated area with a tight bandage or wrap unless your doctor tells you to. Avoid getting it in your eyes, mouth, or nose. 
• INJECTION: This will be given to you by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital — you will not give this to yourself at home. 
• TABLETS or LIQUID (oral form): Take by mouth with food or milk to help prevent stomach upset. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water.
dosing:
Your dose will depend on your condition, the form of betamethasone you are using, and your age. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. 
• SKIN (topical) products: Usually applied 1 to 2 times per day to the affected area. Do not use more than directed and do not use it for longer than prescribed — overuse can thin the skin. 
• ORAL (by mouth): Doses vary widely. Your doctor will tell you exactly how many tablets or how much liquid to take and how often. 
• INJECTION: Given by your doctor or nurse — dosing is determined by your healthcare provider. 
Never increase your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose:
• TOPICAL (skin) products: If you forget to apply a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one and continue with your regular schedule. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed dose. 
• ORAL (by mouth): If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for one you missed. 
• If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage:
• Store betamethasone cream, ointment, lotion, or tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). 
• Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. 
• Keep the lid or cap tightly closed when not in use. 
• Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. 
• Do not freeze the cream, ointment, or lotion. 
• Do not use after the expiration date printed on the package. 
• Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid:
• Do not apply topical betamethasone to your face, groin, armpits, or under the breasts unless your doctor specifically tells you to — the skin in these areas absorbs the medication more and side effects are more likely. 
• Do not use betamethasone on open wounds, infected skin, or broken skin unless your doctor directs you to. 
• Avoid getting the cream or ointment in your eyes. If this happens, rinse with water right away. 
• Do not use more than the amount prescribed or for a longer time than prescribed. 
• Do not wear tight clothing or plastic wrap over treated skin unless told to by your doctor. 
• Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as chickenpox or MMR) while using betamethasone, especially if you are taking it by mouth or injection — ask your doctor first. 
• Avoid close contact with people who have chickenpox, measles, or other contagious illnesses, as steroids can weaken your immune system. 
• Do not stop taking oral betamethasone suddenly without talking to your doctor — the dose usually needs to be slowly reduced.
when_to_call_doctor:
Call your doctor or seek medical help right away if you notice any of the following: 
• Signs of a skin infection where you are applying the cream: increased redness, warmth, swelling, pain, or pus 
• Skin becomes very thin, bruises easily, or develops stretch marks or unusual discoloration 
• Severe burning, stinging, or irritation of the skin after applying 
• Vision changes or eye pain 
• Signs of high blood sugar (increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision) — especially important for people with diabetes 
• Swelling of the hands, ankles, or feet 
• Unusual weight gain 
• Mood changes, depression, or feeling confused 
• Signs of a serious allergic reaction: rash, severe itching, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing 
• If you are pregnant and are receiving injections — monitor for unusual symptoms and report them right away 
• If your condition does not improve after a few weeks of treatment
when_it_works:
• TOPICAL (skin): You may start to notice improvement in redness, itching, and swelling within a few days of starting treatment. Full improvement may take 1 to 2 weeks depending on your skin condition. 
• ORAL or INJECTION: Effects are usually felt within a few hours to a few days, depending on the condition being treated. 
• Keep using the medication as directed even if you feel better early, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations:
• PREGNANCY: Betamethasone injections are sometimes intentionally given to pregnant women at risk of early delivery to help the baby's lungs develop. However, regular long-term use of topical or oral betamethasone during pregnancy should be discussed carefully with your doctor as it may carry risks. 
• BREASTFEEDING: Small amounts of betamethasone may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before using this medication if you are breastfeeding. 
• CHILDREN: Children are more sensitive to the effects of corticosteroids. Topical betamethasone should be used in children only as directed by a doctor, for the shortest time needed, and in the smallest effective amount. It should generally not be used on the face in children. Growth should be monitored in children using steroid medicines long-term. 
• OLDER ADULTS (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as skin thinning, easy bruising, and bone loss. Use the lowest effective amount for the shortest time possible. 
• PEOPLE WITH DIABETES: Betamethasone can raise blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood sugar more closely and report any changes to your doctor. 
• PEOPLE WITH INFECTIONS: Steroids can mask the signs of infection and may make infections harder to fight. Tell your doctor about any active infections before starting this medication.
